1:
What occasion the psalm belongs to is disputed from the first line. John Calvin, Matthew Henry and Keil and Delitzsch all take the title at its word and set the psalm at the night when Saul sent a party of his guards to beset David’s house. Henry notes that the hostility was newly begun, David having just narrowly escaped Saul’s javelin, and admires that these first eruptions of malice did not put him out of frame for prayer and praises — happy are those whose intercourse with heaven is not intercepted by their cares or griefs or fears. Calvin sketches the whole movement from that starting point: David insists on the injustice of a hostility he had done nothing to deserve, follows the complaint with prayer, then as his hopes revive proceeds to prophesy his enemies’ destruction, and at the close engages to remember his deliverance with thanks. Keil and Delitzsch qualify the title, which no more implies the psalm was composed on that very night, made possible by Michal’s artifice, than a comparable inscription implies another psalm was written at the moment the prophet arrived; the preposition of such headings sets forth only in a general way the historical groundwork of the song. They add that this is the earliest of the Davidic psalms dated from the time of Saul’s persecution.

Adam Clarke rejects the setting outright. When the reader considers the whole psalm carefully, he says, he will be convinced that the title does not correspond to the contents, since scarcely anything in it can apply to Saul’s sending; and he reads the workers of iniquity as the enemies of the returned captives — Sanballat, Tobiah and Geshem — who four several times endeavoured to bring Nehemiah into an ambush that they might take his life. He treats the first half of the heading as carrying no more weight, supposing that it may mean only that the psalm is to be sung to the tune of an earlier one bearing the same words.

Augustine of Hippo makes the heading the door of the whole. As Scripture is wont to set the mysteries of the psalms on their titles and to deck the brow of a psalm with the high announcement of a mystery, so that those about to go in may read on the door-post what is doing within and know whose the house is, so this psalm has a title of a title, since it says corrupt not, unto the inscription of the title. What that inscription is the Gospel indicates: when the Lord was being crucified a title was written and set up by Pilate, King of the Jews, in the three tongues which mostly prevail in the whole world — and it is the corrupting of that which the psalm forbids.

The petitions themselves are read from the danger. C.H. Spurgeon pictures the house surrounded, the men outside carrying the warrant of authority and a force equal to carrying it out, David to be taken dead or alive, with no prowess able to break the cordon and no eloquence to stay his persecutor; he was taken like a bird in a net, and unbelief would have suggested that prayer was a waste of breath, but he makes it his sole resort, crying for deliverance and leaving ways and means with his God. Charles Ellicott renders the second verb literally as set me on high, that is, place me on some lofty and secure height. John Gill widens the reference in three directions at once: David had enemies from his youth, and the very qualities that should have won him favour made Saul his enemy; Christ had his enemies though he went about doing good; and the church has hers in sin, Satan and the world — and as David and Christ had a covenant God to go to, so has she.
3:
The ambush is described in military terms. Charles Ellicott would render the opening not as lying in wait but as for look, they have laid an ambush, takes mighty as carrying the idea of insolence in their strength, and reads the next clause as without transgression or fault of mine. C.H. Spurgeon keeps the picture and turns it to prayer: they were in ambuscade for the good man’s life, crouching like wild beasts to make the fatal spring, but their victim baffled them by laying the matter before the Lord — while the enemy lies waiting in the posture of a beast, we wait before God in the posture of prayer. He notices too what kind of men were engaged: the men at arms who ought to have been fighting their country’s battles were instead hunting a quiet citizen, and the monarch was spending all his strength to slay a faithful follower. John Gill presses the word soul, so precious that its redemption cost the blood of Christ, and widens the ambush through the Scriptures, from the men who watched the house to those who sought the life of Christ, to Satan’s wiles and the false teachers who lie in wait to deceive. John Wesley explains the running as to and fro, to receive Saul’s commands and execute them with speed; Adam Clarke keeps his own setting, that they leave no stone unturned to effect his destruction and prevent the building.

On the plea of innocence C.H. Spurgeon observes the repetition and draws a rule from it. David appeals to Jehovah that he had done no ill, his only fault being that he was too valiant and too gracious and besides the chosen of the Lord, so that the envious king could not rest till he had washed his hands in his rival’s blood; and we shall always find it a great thing to be innocent, for if it does not carry our cause before an earthly tribunal it will prove the best of arguments in the court of conscience.

Who is prayed against divides them. Charles Ellicott insists that the heathen and the wicked transgressors are not synonymous but contrasted, since there were domestic as well as foreign foes — men who pretended to be loyal Israelites while intriguing with the foreigners — and the literal coverers of wickedness implies concealment and treachery. John Wesley makes the same distinction from the other side, that these are Israelites by birth yet in their dispositions mere heathens. C.H. Spurgeon agrees, asking God to punish the heathen among his Israel, the falsehearted who say they are Jews and are not. Adam Clarke keeps the foreign sense, a handful of distressed captives surrounded by heathen chiefs, and renders the phrase changers of iniquity, men who go the whole round of evil.

Whether such a petition can be prayed at all is answered three ways. C.H. Spurgeon divides the request: be merciful to them as men, but not as transgressors, for if God winks at their oppression the righteous are left under their power. John Wesley answers from God’s own word, that indeed he cannot be merciful to such incorrigible offenders. Adam Clarke answers from parallel, that the prayer is exactly the same in sentiment as the one Nehemiah offered against his enemies. C.H. Spurgeon adds a note on the piling up of divine titles: it is the mark of a thoughtful prayer when the names applied to God are congruous to the matter and add force to the argument — shall the God of hosts permit his enemies to exult over his servant? Charles Ellicott hears the same accumulation as passion, the prayer unable to exhaust itself without piling up all the customary names; John Gill unfolds one of them, the God of the armies of heaven and of all the inhabitants of the earth.
6:
The returning at evening is read four ways. John Wesley keeps it literal: the watchers waited all night and, not finding him at home, sought him elsewhere in the city. Adam Clarke makes it seasonal, the hour when beasts of prey leave their dens and prowl about cities to entrap domestic animals, so these come round the city to see whether they may get entrance and destroy the work. C.H. Spurgeon keeps the animal figure and adds the outcome: David compares his foes to Eastern dogs, lean and hungry, howling with disappointment because they cannot find the food they seek, the watchmen having raged when they found the image and the pillow of goats’ hair in the bed — go, he says, ye dogs, to your kennels and gnaw your bones, for this good man is not meat for your jaws. John Gill parses the verb three ways at once: as a statement of what the messengers did, as a wish that they may return in shame, and as a prophecy true of all the wicked, who shall return from their graves at the evening of the day of the Lord.

Charles Ellicott supplies the natural history, the gaunt half-starved wild dogs of an Eastern town, and would render the verb howl. He supports it with a traveller’s account of a night in Constantinople, where the whole city rang with one vast riot and the sixty thousand dogs said to overrun the place seemed bent on exterminating each other, the yelping and snarling merged into one continuous sound. On the next verse he proposes reading the word rendered behold as spears: spears they pour out with their mouths, swords with their lips. John Gill renders the same verb as bubbling out, like water from a fountain; C.H. Spurgeon agrees that the wicked are voluble in slander and speak daggers; Adam Clarke lists the weapons as sarcasm, ridicule and lies; and John Wesley supplies their reasoning, that David does not hear us, and God either does not hear or does not regard.

The laughter of God is the turn of the psalm. C.H. Spurgeon hears David speaking to God as to one close at hand and pointing out the men in ambush: they are laughing at me, but thou hast the laugh of them, having determined to send them away without their victim; the most malicious enemies of the church are only objects of ridicule to the Lord. John Gill and Adam Clarke both take the laughter as the disappointing of their counsels, Gill instancing the image in the bed, Clarke that God will turn their schemes into ridicule.

The next clause is disputed in its text. Adam Clarke says that with the received reading he can make no sense of the passage, and prefers my strength, supported by fourteen manuscripts and the versions: to God he commits all his strength and from him derives all he has. Charles Ellicott agrees that his strength gives no intelligible meaning, holds that the closing verse shows the versions right in reading my strength as a vocative, and would carry the first two words of the next verse back into this one. C.H. Spurgeon keeps the received text and makes the strength the persecutor’s: is my persecutor strong? then for that reason I will turn to thee and leave my matters in thy hand, since it is wise to find in the greatness of our difficulties a reason for casting ourselves on the Lord. Matthew Henry allows both, either the strength of his enemies, the fear of which drove him to God, or God’s strength, the hope of which drew him; and he dwells rather on the next title, that it is comfortable to eye God not only as the God of mercy but as the God of our mercy, whatever mercy is in him being laid up for us.
11:
Why the psalmist should ask that his enemies not be slain is the difficulty, and the answers differ in kind. Adam Clarke follows the Chaldee and makes it a matter of speed rather than severity: do not slay them suddenly, but drive them from their habitations and reduce them to poverty, preserving them long in chastisement so that Israel may see God’s hand on the wicked for evil and on themselves for good — as the Canaanites were left to be pricks in the eyes and thorns in the sides of Israel. John Gill reads it as intercession, agreeing with Christ’s petition from the cross, and offers two senses: slay them not directly, but give them space for repentance, since forty years passed before the destruction came; or slay them not utterly, since many were carried captive rather than killed and their posterity continue to this day. John Wesley puts the emphasis on the scattering: they wander from place to place carrying the tokens of God’s justice and their own shame. C.H. Spurgeon argues from the certainty of the outcome: it argues great faith that, with his house surrounded, David is so sure of their overthrow that he asks they may not be exterminated too soon, since God’s victory over the craft of the wicked is so easy and so glorious that it seems a pity to end the conflict too early. Let the boasting oppressor puff and brag through his little hour, he says; it will keep Israel in mind of the Lord’s justice. He adds two maxims: it were a pity for good men to be without detractors, since virtue shines the brighter for the foil of slander, and a lively, vexatious devil is less to be dreaded than a sleepy, forgetful spirit.

Charles Ellicott alone treats the request as a moral question. National feeling, he observes, has often insisted on extreme modes of punishment, partly vindictive and partly deterrent; but where is the parallel to what seems uppermost in the psalmist’s mind, a wish for protracted retribution on the nations for the moral benefit of Israel? The nearest he can find are the Spartans, who refused to destroy a neighbouring city that had often called out their armies, saying, destroy not the whetstone of our young men; and a stage curse that a hated city might live loathed and long. He would also render the next verb make them wander, a word used of Cain and of Israel in the wilderness.

The following clause is disputed in construction. John Gill would read the two phrases as one proposition, that the words of their lips are the sin of their mouth. Charles Ellicott calls that tautological nonsense and prefers to take the nouns as adverbs of instrument: by the sin of their mouth, by the word of their lips, let them be taken in their pride; the second half he reads as asking that their own slanders recoil on their own heads, a frequent thought in the Psalms. John Wesley supplies the content plainly: their proud speeches against God and their lying reports of David.

Adam Clarke reaches a different sense by taking the word for sin as sin-offering. Some of Nehemiah’s enemies professed the Jewish religion and were allied by marriage to the Jews; the priest had even given Tobiah one of the great chambers of the house of the Lord, where the meat-offerings and the tithes had been kept, so that offerings meant for the Levites were consumed by his household — and there we have the sin of their mouth. John Gill notes that the repeated demand of the next verse shows the ardour of the petitioner; Charles Ellicott takes the words asking they may be no more closely together, the overthrow of the foes being a proof to the ends of the world of the rule of the God of Jacob.
14:
The refrain returns, and what has changed in it is the question. John Gill says that what was earlier related as matter of fact is here expressed by way of imprecation, so that what was noticed as their sin is now wished as their punishment. Adam Clarke reads the change as one of confidence rather than mood: they had come like beasts of prey striving to get in, but now, assured of God’s protection, he can bid them return and howl like famished creatures about the city-walls; the breaches had been made up and the city so well guarded that there was no longer any fear of surprise, and now they must feel like hungry beasts disappointed of their prey. C.H. Spurgeon hears defiance and something like laughter: the songster revels in their futile search, their disappointment and wasted energy, and laughs to think that all the city would know how they were deceived and all Israel would ring with the story of the image and the goats’ hair in the bed. Nothing, he adds, was more a subject of Oriental merriment than a case in which the crafty are deceived, and nothing makes a man more an object of derision than to be outwitted by a woman, as Saul and his minions were by Michal.

The last clause of the following verse is obscure, and Charles Ellicott alone works at it. The verse is variously understood: the marginal rendering favoured by most modern scholars gives they will pass the night, but what that means is unclear, and to say they will not go away unsatisfied seems poor; one conjecture, that they will satisfy themselves forsooth and remain, meaning die, he calls strained. The slightest change in the vowel-points, however, gives the reading of the ancient versions, if not satisfied they will growl, which he judges to suit the context admirably. C.H. Spurgeon reaches the same picture without the philology: they act like those who cannot believe they have lost their prey, prowling like unhoused dogs after something they shall never find, saying that surely he must be in yonder corner. John Gill puts it in three words, like hungry dogs.

The turn to praise is read as the psalm’s point. C.H. Spurgeon sets the two sounds against each other — the wicked howl, but I sing and will sing — and takes the morning as the hour when the lovers of darkness find their game is up and their midnight howlings die away. What a blessed morning will soon break for the righteous, he says: sons of the morning, ye may sigh tonight, but joy will come on the wings of the rising sun, so tune your harps even now, for the signal to commence the eternal music will soon be given. He draws the same lesson from the trouble itself, that the greater our present trials the louder will our future songs be, since had we no day of trouble we should have no season of retrospective thanksgiving. Adam Clarke makes the singing an acquittal of debt, that he will publish abroad what God has done, not for his own worthiness but for mercy’s sake; on the last verse he presses the possessives one by one — God is my strength, God is my elevation, my God is my mercy — and concludes that all springs from his dwelling in us. John Gill lists what the power sung of includes: creation out of nothing, the upholding of all things, redemption, conversion, preservation, the performance of promises, and the destruction of enemies.

Adam Clarke ends by conceding the ground he has held throughout the psalm. Since many persons may still think the inscription correct, he says, his analysis may be applied in that way instead; or it may be taken as a general resolution of the psalm, without referring it to any particular occasion at all.
